title: No. 69 — The Real Character of the Executive (Hamilton)
paragraphs: I now proceed to trace the real character of the proposed Executive as outlined in the convention's plan. This will help expose the unfairness of the criticisms that have been made against it.

The first thing that strikes us is that executive authority, with few exceptions, will be vested in a single magistrate. This, however, is hardly a point on which any meaningful comparison can be built. If there is a resemblance to the king of Great Britain in this respect, there is just as much resemblance to the Grand Seignior, the khan of Tartary, the Man of the Seven Mountains, or the governor of New York.

This magistrate will be elected for four years, and may be re-elected as often as the people of the United States judge him worthy of their trust. In these circumstances, he is entirely unlike a king of Great Britain, who is a hereditary monarch holding the crown as an inheritance passed down to his heirs forever. But he closely resembles a governor of New York, who is elected for three years and may be re-elected without limit. If we consider how much less time it would take to build a dangerous level of influence in a single state than across the whole United States, we must conclude that a four-year term for the Chief Magistrate of the Union is far less to be feared than a three-year term for the corresponding office in a single state.

The President of the United States could be impeached, tried, and, upon conviction of treason, bribery, or other high crimes or misdemeanors, removed from office. He would then be subject to prosecution and punishment under ordinary law. The person of the king of Great Britain is sacred and inviolable. There is no constitutional tribunal he can be brought before, and no punishment he can suffer without provoking a national revolution. On this critical matter of personal accountability, the President of Confederated America stands on no better footing than a governor of New York, and on worse footing than the governors of Maryland and Delaware.

The President of the United States will have power to return a bill, after it has passed both branches of the legislature, for reconsideration. The bill so returned becomes law if, on reconsideration, two-thirds of both houses approve it. The king of Great Britain, by contrast, has an absolute veto over the acts of both houses of Parliament. The disuse of that power for a long time does not affect its real existence. It is to be explained entirely by the fact that the crown has found ways to substitute influence for authority — gaining a majority in one or the other house, rather than exercising a prerogative that could rarely be used without risking some national upheaval. The President's qualified veto differs widely from this absolute veto of the British sovereign. It corresponds exactly to the revisionary authority of this state's council of revision, of which the governor is part. In this respect the President's power would exceed that of the governor of New York. The President would hold alone what the governor shares with the chancellor and judges. But it would be precisely the same as the power of the governor of Massachusetts, whose constitution on this point seems to have been the model the convention copied.

The President is to be the "commander-in-chief of the army and navy of the United States, and of the militia of the several States, when called into the actual service of the United States. He is to have power to grant reprieves and pardons for offenses against the United States, except in cases of impeachment; to recommend to Congress such measures as he judges necessary and expedient; to convene, on extraordinary occasions, both houses of the legislature, or either of them, and, in case of disagreement between them about adjournment, to adjourn them to such time as he thinks proper; to take care that the laws are faithfully executed; and to commission all officers of the United States." In most of these particulars, the President's power resembles equally that of the king of Great Britain and that of the governor of New York. The most important differences are these: First. The President will only have occasional command of those parts of the militia called into actual service of the Union by legislative provision. The king of Great Britain and the governor of New York have at all times complete command of all militia within their jurisdictions. On this point, the President's power would be inferior to either the monarch's or the governor's. Second. The President is to be commander-in-chief of the army and navy of the United States. In this respect his authority is nominally the same as the king of Great Britain's, but in substance much weaker. It amounts only to the supreme command and direction of the military and naval forces, as first General and admiral of the Confederacy. The British king's authority extends to declaring war and to raising and regulating fleets and armies — all of which, under the proposed Constitution, would belong to the legislature.(1) The governor of New York, in contrast, is given by the state constitution only command of its militia and navy. But several state constitutions explicitly declare their governors to be commanders-in-chief of both army and navy. It may well be a question whether those of New Hampshire and Massachusetts, in particular, do not in this respect grant their governors larger powers than could be claimed by a President of the United States. Third. The President's power of pardon would extend to all cases except impeachment. The governor of New York may pardon in all cases, even impeachment, except for treason and murder. On this point, considering political consequences, is the governor's power not greater than the President's? All conspiracies and plots against the government, before they ripen into actual treason, could be shielded from any punishment by the prerogative of pardon. If a governor of New York were the head of such a conspiracy, he could, until the design ripened into open hostilities, guarantee complete impunity to his accomplices and supporters. A President of the Union, by contrast, even if he could pardon treason when prosecuted under ordinary law, could not shield any offender from impeachment and conviction. Would not the prospect of total immunity for all preliminary steps be a greater temptation to undertake and persist in a plot against public liberty than the mere prospect of escaping death and confiscation if the final scheme, on actual recourse to arms, should fail? Would this last expectation carry any weight at all, when one considers the probability that the very person granting the exemption might himself be entangled in the consequences and rendered incapable of granting it? To judge this matter properly, we must remember that under the proposed Constitution, treason is limited "to levying war upon the United States, and adhering to their enemies, giving them aid and comfort"; and that under New York law it is similarly bounded. Fourth. The President can adjourn the national legislature only when there is disagreement about the time of adjournment. The British monarch may prorogue or even dissolve Parliament. The governor of New York may also prorogue this state's legislature for a limited time — a power that, in certain situations, may serve very important purposes.

The President is to have power, with the advice and consent of the Senate, to make treaties, provided two-thirds of the senators present concur. The king of Great Britain is the sole and absolute representative of the nation in all foreign matters. He can on his own authority make treaties of peace, commerce, alliance, and every other kind. It has been suggested that his authority in this respect is not final, and that his agreements with foreign powers must be revised and ratified by Parliament. But I believe this doctrine was never heard of until it was raised on the present occasion. Every jurist(2) of that kingdom, and every other person familiar with its Constitution, knows as established fact that the prerogative of making treaties rests in the crown in its fullest extent. The agreements made under royal authority have complete legal validity and force without any other approval. Parliament, it is true, sometimes alters existing laws to bring them into conformity with the terms of a new treaty. This may have given rise to the impression that its cooperation was needed for the treaty's binding force. But this parliamentary action arises from a different cause: the necessity of adjusting an artificial and intricate system of revenue and commercial laws to the changes the treaty creates, and of adapting new provisions and safeguards to the new state of affairs, to keep the machine from falling into disorder. So in this respect there is no comparison between the proposed power of the President and the actual power of the British sovereign. The one can do alone what the other can do only with the agreement of a branch of the legislature. It must be admitted that on this point the federal Executive's power would exceed that of any state Executive. But this follows naturally from the sovereign authority that pertains to treaties. If the Confederacy were to dissolve, it would become a question whether the Executives of the several states would not be solely vested with this delicate and important prerogative.

The President is also authorized to receive ambassadors and other public ministers. This, though it has been a rich subject for declamation, is more a matter of dignity than of authority. It is a circumstance with no real consequence in the administration of government. It was far more convenient to arrange it this way than to require the legislature, or one of its branches, to convene whenever a foreign minister arrived — even merely to replace a departed predecessor.

The President is to nominate, and, with the advice and consent of the Senate, appoint ambassadors and other public ministers, judges of the Supreme Court, and generally all officers of the United States established by law whose appointments are not otherwise provided for by the Constitution. The king of Great Britain is emphatically and truly called the fountain of honor. He not only fills all offices but can create offices. He can confer titles of nobility at his pleasure, and has the disposal of an immense number of church appointments. The President's power in this respect is plainly far inferior to the British king's, and is not equal even to that of the governor of New York, if we interpret this state's constitution by the practice that has prevailed under it. Among us, the appointing power lies with a council made up of the governor and four senators chosen by the Assembly. The governor claims, and has often exercised, the right of nomination, and is entitled to a tie-breaking vote in the appointment. If he really has the right of nomination, his authority equals the President's on this point, and exceeds it in the matter of the tie-breaking vote. In the national government, if the Senate is divided, no appointment can be made. In the New York government, if the council is divided, the governor can tip the scale and confirm his own nomination.(3) If we compare the publicity that must surround appointment by the President and an entire branch of the national legislature with the secrecy of appointment by the governor of New York — closeted in a private room with at most four people, and often with only two — and if we also consider how much easier it must be to influence the small number on a council of appointment than the much larger number on the national Senate, we cannot hesitate to conclude that the chief magistrate of this state, in disposing of offices, must in practice hold far greater power than the Chief Magistrate of the Union.

Thus it appears that, except for the President's shared authority over treaties, it would be hard to say whether that magistrate would, on the whole, have more or less power than the Governor of New York. And it appears even more clearly that there is no basis for the parallel that has been attempted between him and the king of Great Britain. But to make the contrast even more striking, it may help to bring the main points of difference into a tighter group.

The President of the United States would be an officer elected by the people for four years; the king of Great Britain is a perpetual and hereditary prince. The one would be subject to personal punishment and disgrace; the person of the other is sacred and inviolable. The one would have a qualified veto on legislative acts; the other has an absolute veto. The one would have the right to command the military and naval forces of the nation; the other, in addition, possesses the right of declaring war and of raising and regulating fleets and armies on his own authority. The one would have a concurrent power with a branch of the legislature in making treaties; the other is the sole possessor of the treaty-making power. The one would have similar concurrent authority in appointing to offices; the other is the sole author of all appointments. The one can confer no privileges whatever; the other can naturalize aliens, ennoble commoners, and erect corporations with all the rights belonging to corporate bodies. The one can prescribe no rules concerning the nation's commerce or currency; the other is in several respects the arbiter of commerce, and in that capacity can establish markets and fairs, regulate weights and measures, lay embargoes for a limited time, coin money, and authorize or prohibit the circulation of foreign coin. The one has no scrap of spiritual jurisdiction; the other is the supreme head and governor of the national church! What answer shall we give to those who try to persuade us that things so unlike resemble each other? The same answer we should give to those who tell us that a government whose entire power is in the hands of the elective and periodic servants of the people is an aristocracy, a monarchy, and a despotism.

1. A writer in a Pennsylvania paper, under the signature of TAMONY, has claimed that the king of Great Britain owes his prerogative as commander-in-chief to an annual mutiny bill. The truth is the opposite: his prerogative in this respect is immemorial, and was only disputed, "contrary to all reason and precedent," as Blackstone (vol. i, p. 262) puts it, by the Long Parliament of Charles I. By the statute 13 Charles II, chap. 6, it was declared to be in the king alone, for the sole supreme government and command of the militia within his Majesty's realms and dominions, and of all forces by sea and land, and of all forts and places of strength, EVER WAS AND IS the undoubted right of his Majesty and his royal predecessors, kings and queens of England, and that neither house of Parliament can or ought to claim the same.
2. See Blackstone's Commentaries, Vol. I, p. 257.

3. Candor, however, requires me to admit that I do not think the governor's claim to a right of nomination is well founded. Still, it is always legitimate to reason from the actual practice of a government until its propriety has been constitutionally questioned. And even setting aside this claim, when we take into account the other considerations and follow them through all their consequences, we will be inclined to draw much the same conclusion.
